title: Reform networks: Background shapes but cannot determine innovation
desc: Explains investment-treaty reform through professional paradigms, insider–outsider roles and institutional access to expertise.

kps.k: Professional backgrounds and networks shape how actors understand investment treaty arbitration and imagine its reform.
kps.d: The cluster treats legal development as more than a response to treaty text or states’ economic interests. In Clash of Paradigms, Roberts argues that training supplies familiar legal analogies, while competition over relevant expertise distributes professional authority. Roberts and St John extend this argument to officials’ reform proposals: proximity to arbitration practice tends to favour improvements within the system, while distance can encourage institutional replacement. The BRICS fragment adds only a secondary report of Dezalay and Garth’s account of socialization into elite networks and Western arbitration norms; it supplies no independent empirical detail.

qs.q: Pierre Bourdieu uses the notion of “symbolic capital”—which includes factors such as education, career, knowledge, reputation, and expertise—to explain the relative power of different participants within a given field.57 How participants understand and characterize the system, including through their choice of analogies, can influence the distribution of symbolic capital.
qs.a: Clash of Paradigms: Actors and Analogies Shaping the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2013

kps.k: Competing legal paradigms produce different answers about authority, transparency and regulatory protection.
kps.d: Roberts describes a hybrid system with a treaty foundation, arbitral procedures and public regulatory consequences. Commercial arbitration emphasizes equality between investor and host state and disputing-party autonomy; public international law privileges treaty states; public-law approaches emphasize regulatory authority and public participation. These are substantive disagreements, not interchangeable labels. Roberts links early commercial influence to investor appointments and commercially rooted institutions, but also argues that public-law models can obscure the treaty basis and choice of arbitration. Her cited ICSID transparency and participation reforms show public-oriented change without complete conversion into a court system.

qs.q: The public international law paradigm, for instance, focuses attention on the system’s treaty basis, thereby putting the treaty parties in a position of relative superiority to both investors (who are not treaty parties) and investment tribunals (which are presented as agents of the treaty parties).
qs.a: Clash of Paradigms: Actors and Analogies Shaping the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2013

qs.q: The commercial arbitration par- adigm, by contrast, focuses attention on the disputing parties and emphasizes that the investor and host state are disputants subject to “equality of arms,” which tends to downgrade the rel- ative significance of states and elevate that of investors.
qs.a: Clash of Paradigms: Actors and Analogies Shaping the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2013

kps.k: The insider–outsider distinction helps explain the direction of innovation, not whether actors innovate at all.
kps.d: Roberts and St John draw on five years of para-ethnographic observation and interviews, using the EU, USA, Brazil and Bahrain as case studies. They associate the EU’s investment-court proposal with outsider Commission officials, responsibility allocated to DG Trade and experience with the WTO. The proposal would replace investor-state arbitration while retaining substantive treaty obligations. By contrast, they describe arbitration-experienced US officials as innovators within the existing system. Brazil’s outsider representation and Bahrain’s practitioner representation illustrate the same pattern, although their different policy histories and arbitration ambitions also matter.

qs.q: However, the background  of the officials - including their relative distance from investor-state arbitration but  their proximity to the WTO system - played a key role in the ISDS reform proposal that  the European Commission ended up adopting.
qs.a: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2022

kps.k: Disagreement over insiders and outsiders concerns both legitimate expertise and the strength of causal explanations.
kps.d: Roberts recounts practitioners questioning critical academics’ arbitration expertise, while Van Harten defended outsiders’ independence and broader public-policy knowledge. Overlapping academic and practitioner roles can transfer ideas but also create self-censorship and neutrality concerns. Roberts and St John acknowledge scholarship challenging the elite-club image and a larger, more diverse arbitrator pool. Neither analysis makes background determinative: Roberts flags the difficulty of proving effects on adjudication; Roberts and St John recognize feedback between policy and hiring, alongside economic position, ideology and experience with disputes. Their argument does not establish that outsiders produce better reforms.

qs.q: This statement received a hostile reaction from many investment treaty arbitration lawyers, with a commonly voiced criticism being that the signatories lacked relevant expertise in invest- ment treaty law and arbitral practice.
qs.a: Clash of Paradigms: Actors and Analogies Shaping the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2013

qs.q: A state’s general ISDS policy and officials’ backgrounds are endogenous - that is,  there are feedback loops connecting earlier policy decisions to later personnel deci- sions, which in turn shape subsequent policy decisions and so on.
qs.a: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2022

kps.k: Institutional design influences which expertise enters decision-making and can reinforce either continuity or change.
kps.d: Roberts identifies appointment mechanisms, screened rosters, specialist qualifications, restrictions on simultaneous counsel and arbitrator roles, and standing or appellate bodies as ways states could alter the decision-making community. She predicts substantive consequences rather than demonstrating that every option produces them. Roberts and St John locate a parallel mechanism within governments: assigning policy to particular agencies selects officials with different backgrounds, while small teams and weak checks may amplify individual preferences. Together, the analyses make staffing, appointment rules and administrative allocation relevant to reform design, not merely implementation details.

qs.q: If states wish to shift the backgrounds of arbitrators more significantly, they can do so by changing the mechanisms for appointment or the rules for challenging appointments.183 For example, if states were to determine that lawyers could not serve as counsel and as arbitrators, this would change the composition of the arbitral field because most serving law firm partners

qs.q: Choices of whether to locate responsibility in one ministry or  agency or level of government over another likely make a difference as to which of- ficials work on the policy area and what their backgrounds are.
qs.a: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2022

kps.k: Original proposals, successful adoption and durable reform require separate explanations.
kps.d: Roberts and St John caution that outsiders’ weaker networks may impede coalition-building; they observe that sustained attendance and substantive contributions increase proposals’ standing, while leaving diffusion and adoption unresolved. Roberts likewise predicts contested adaptation rather than an inevitable public-law takeover: arbitrators may accommodate states to preserve the system, while investors and practitioners pursue counterstrategies. Her practical recommendation is to combine perspectives to address their respective blind spots. Limited amicus participation illustrates such a hybrid: public participation expands, but disputing parties’ responsibility for arbitrator costs constrains full convergence with courts.

qs.q: Fourth, our argument about outsiders is limited to proposing reforms; the same out- sider traits that contribute to the development of disruptive reforms (such as a lack of  networks within the field) may make it harder for these individuals to convince others  to support their proposed reforms.
qs.a: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2022

qs.q: If arbitrators perceive the threat of exit and recontracting by states to be significant, they will have increased incentives to accommodate states’ preferences, including as to paradigms and analogies.
qs.a: Clash of Paradigms: Actors and Analogies Shaping the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2013

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources support the proposition that professional backgrounds, paradigms and networks shape—but do not determine—how investment-treaty actors understand the system and pursue reform. Roberts and St John provide the strongest direct evidence: their observation-and-interview research associates outsider officials with disruptive proposals and arbitration insiders with sustaining innovation, while treating background as one factor alongside state position, ideology, policy history and institutional allocation. Roberts supplies the conceptual mechanism, arguing that professional training makes particular legal frames and analogies appear natural, but she stresses that effects on adjudication are empirically difficult to establish. The BRICS fragment is directionally consistent through its report of socialization into elite arbitration networks and Western norms, but it is derivative and too incomplete to add a developed causal account. Material variation therefore concerns evidentiary strength and scope rather than overall position: one source comparatively examines government officials and proposal formation; another develops a broader paradigmatic and institutional analysis while favouring hybrid reform; and the fragment offers only limited secondary support. These curated sources should not be taken as representative of academic opinion generally.

qs.q: As an empirical matter, it is difficult to prove what impact, if any, arbitrators’ backgrounds will have on their approaches to investor-state disputes.
qs.a: Clash of Paradigms: Actors and Analogies Shaping the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2013

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources support the proposition’s foundational claim that professional backgrounds, networks and legal paradigms shape—but do not determine—understandings of investment treaty arbitration and possible reform. Roberts provides the principal developed argument: lawyers’ training makes certain analogies appear natural; competing paradigms distribute authority differently; and appointment structures influence which forms of expertise enter decision-making. She also expressly limits the causal claim, noting that background effects are empirically difficult to prove and may interact with mixed professional identities, client interests and strategic adaptation. The BRICS fragment points in the same direction through its report of lawyers’ socialization into elite arbitration networks and adoption of Western norms, but its support is narrow and derivative because the fragment supplies neither independent evidence nor a developed causal analysis. This period therefore establishes the cluster’s conceptual and institutional foundations, but it does not yet provide the later comparative evidence linking government officials’ insider or outsider status to sustaining versus disruptive reform proposals.

qs.q: As an empirical matter, it is difficult to prove what impact, if any, arbitrators’ backgrounds will have on their approaches to investor-state disputes.
qs.a: Clash of Paradigms: Actors and Analogies Shaping the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2013

elens.an: The 2015–2022 evidence supports the proposition that professional background, insider–outsider position and institutional allocation shape the direction of investment-treaty reform without determining it. Based on observation and interviews, the source associates officials distant from investment-arbitration practice with disruptive proposals and insiders with reforms that sustain the existing system. Its comparisons also show material internal variation: outsider EU officials pursued replacement of arbitration with a multilateral investment court, whereas arbitration-experienced US officials innovated within ISDS; Brazil and Bahrain are presented as further illustrations. The account is explicitly probabilistic rather than deterministic: economic position, ideology, prior ISDS experience, arbitration-hub ambitions and feedback between policy and personnel also matter. It further distinguishes generating an original proposal from securing its adoption, and does not claim that disruptive reforms are better. Because this time-period subset contains one curated source, it supplies direct support but does not establish how prevalent this view was among scholars or officials.

qs.q: Our argument  is that outsider status increases the chances that officials will develop disruptive in- novations, as one of a number of factors influencing state policy.
qs.a: The Originality of Outsiders: Innovation in the Investment Treaty System · Academia · 2022
